# The Last Bus to Bell Street

The bus reached Bell Street at 11:47 every night, unless there was snow, a parade, an accident on the bridge, or the sort of rain that made the traffic lights blink yellow for no apparent reason. By then its windows were usually dark mirrors. Mara could see her own face in the glass, laid over the sleeping storefronts and the thin bands of light under apartment doors.

Bell Street was the end of the line. She waited there for seven minutes, then crossed to the other side of the road and began the return trip. In fourteen years of driving the 6, she had spent enough time at that stop to learn which upstairs neighbors watched television late, which windows held plants through the winter, and when the bakery replaced its sign. She knew less about the people inside those rooms than she knew about the man who boarded each Thursday carrying an empty birdcage.

On her last night, the cage was occupied.

“New bird?” she asked as he climbed aboard.

“Same bird,” he said. “First time she’s agreed to travel.”

He held up the cage. A small gray parrot regarded Mara with one polished eye.

“Where’s she going?”

“Home. She’s been at my sister’s.” He lowered his voice. “I told my sister I missed her.”

“The bird?”

“That’s what I let her think.”

He tapped his card and sat behind the front wheel well. The parrot made a noise like someone trying to start a lawn mower. Mara pulled away from the curb.

The 6 had once gone all the way to the brickworks, when there was still a brickworks. It had once turned at the hospital, before the hospital moved uphill. Next Monday, the route would be folded into two others. The new buses would come more often during the day and not at all after ten. That was the part Mara’s passengers talked about. Everyone understood that a faster trip downtown was useful. They also understood what time the kitchens closed, and what time the second shift ended at the care home.

The transit authority had offered Mara a place on the new route. She had chosen the 23 instead: mornings, a shorter loop, two elementary schools and a supermarket. People congratulated her on the sensible hours. She agreed that they were sensible. She had also grown used to finishing work when most people were asleep, and she wasn’t sure what she would do with an evening.

At the next stop, a woman in green kitchen trousers boarded with a paper bag held carefully upright.

“Last one,” the woman said.

“Last one.”

“That’s a shame.”

Mara waited while she found her fare card. She had never learned the woman’s name. For years they had discussed the weather, a loose tile at the bus stop, the price of oranges, and once the woman’s mother, who had turned ninety and wanted to climb a ladder to clean the gutters. Tonight the woman took a seat halfway back, the bag settled on her knees.

At the station, six passengers came aboard together. The train from the airport had been late. They stood under the shelter looking at their phones and then at the destination sign, uncertain that a bus could be going where they needed to go at this hour. One asked if Mara stopped near Hanover Court. Another needed North Mill Lane. A young man with a silver suitcase named a hotel Mara had never heard of.

“It might be new,” he said.

“Most things are new to someone,” Mara said, and gave him directions from the closest stop.

The last person onto the bus was an older woman pulling a grocery trolley. Its wheels squeaked at different pitches. Mara lowered the bus and watched her cross the gap from curb to floor. The woman thanked her without looking up. Mara knew her as Mrs. Vale, although she had never been told whether that was her name. Once, years ago, a neighbor had called it across the street.

The bus climbed out of the station and passed the dark windows of the post office. At the first red light, Mara heard a tapping near the front of the bus. She checked the mirror. The parrot’s owner was holding one finger against the cage bars. The bird had its head tilted toward him.

They continued through the old shopping district. A few years earlier, the council had put lantern-shaped lights above the street. Most of the shops closed at six, leaving them to illuminate a long row of metal shutters. Tonight a florist was still working inside her shop. Through the window Mara could see buckets of flowers and someone moving between them, lifting stems into bunches. She had passed this shop thousands of times and never been inside.

Mrs. Vale rang the bell for Ash Lane. Mara drew in close to the curb. The grocery trolley caught briefly on the door frame, then rolled free.

“Thank you,” Mrs. Vale said.

“You’re welcome.”

Mrs. Vale looked at the route sign above the windshield. “I suppose I’ll have to find another way on Monday.”

“There’s the 12. It goes down Market Road.”

“I know.”

Market Road was four blocks away. Mrs. Vale took hold of her trolley and set off along Ash Lane. Mara watched until she reached the streetlamp at the corner, then closed the doors.

At the end of her first year on the route, Mara had tried to memorize the regular passengers. It had seemed like part of doing the job well. The effort soon defeated her. People changed jobs, changed coats, went away for months and appeared again. They brought children who grew too tall for free fares. They came aboard carrying flowers or bags from pharmacies, spoke eagerly into phones, or stared at the floor. She learned to recognize some faces without expecting to see them. When a familiar passenger returned after a long absence, she was usually glad.

Near the river, the bus passed the temporary barrier that had replaced the iron railing. A delivery truck had broken through the railing in spring; no one had been hurt, but part of the pavement remained fenced off. The truck was gone long before the repairs were scheduled. Mara had watched weeds grow up between the concrete blocks.

The river itself was high and fast after three days of rain. From the driver’s seat she could see a strip of moving black beneath the bridge lamps. She remembered crossing it with her father when she was little. He had made her count the lamps so she would stop worrying about the traffic below the bus windows. There were eleven. She still counted them sometimes.

A bell sounded. The woman in kitchen trousers came forward with the paper bag.

“Want a roll?” she asked. “They make too many on Fridays.”

“It’s Saturday.”

“We made them yesterday.” She reached into the bag and lifted out a round roll wrapped in a napkin. “Still good.”

Mara took it. It was warm, perhaps from the woman’s hands. “Thank you.”

The woman got off at the care home, went around to the side entrance, and unlocked it. Before the bus moved, she turned and raised a hand. Mara raised hers in return.

By the time they reached the warehouses, the passengers from the station had all gone. The young man with the suitcase had asked twice about his hotel and then recognized its sign from half a block away. Mara waited while he pulled his suitcase over the uneven pavement.

The parrot and its owner remained. So did a student asleep against the window, his headphones hanging around his neck. Mara knew his stop. He had missed it twice in the past month, waking at Bell Street and getting a ride back. At his corner she pulled over and waited. The bus idled. He slept.

“Is this his?” the parrot’s owner asked.

“Yes.”

He leaned across the aisle and touched the student’s shoulder. The student woke with a start, took in the bus stop, and scrambled up.

“Sorry,” he said to both of them.

“No hurry,” Mara told him.

He stepped off, turned around as if checking that he had everything, and found his wallet in his pocket. Then he went toward the apartments above the hardware store.

At Bell Street, Mara set the brake and opened the doors. The parrot’s owner did not move. He lived two stops back, but he often rode to the end if he wanted to finish a conversation. Tonight he was bent over the cage, making a series of soft clicking sounds.

“Seven minutes,” Mara said.

“I know.”

She turned off the interior lights nearest the driver’s seat. Outside, the bakery sign glowed red. The original sign had shown a loaf of bread; the new one had only the name. Mara could remember arriving one night to find the bread gone. She had missed the workers who changed it.

“Are you moving to the 12?” the man asked.

“The 23.”

“Morning route.”

“Yes.”

“You’ll see children, then.”

“I expect so.”

He considered this. “My sister used to drive a school bus. She could tell when a child had lost a tooth before they said anything.”

“How?”

“I never asked.”

The parrot scraped its beak against a perch. Mara unwrapped the roll and took a bite. It had rosemary in it and a few crystals of salt. Across the road, a man came out of the bakery carrying a crate of empty trays. He loaded it into a van, shut the doors, and went back inside.

“What’s her name?” Mara asked, nodding toward the cage.

“Edith.”

“After someone?”

“My sister’s landlord. We named her when we thought she was a boy.” He smiled down at the bird. “By the time we knew better, she knew her name.”

The seven minutes passed. The man carried Edith off the bus, and Mara crossed Bell Street to start back toward the station.

The return trip was quieter. A cleaner boarded outside an office block, then two friends at the cinema, still arguing about the ending of a film. Near the river, a man waved for the bus from the wrong side of the road. Mara pointed across the street to the stop for his direction. He waved again, more vigorously. At the next light she watched him cross safely behind her and disappear toward the shelter.

When Mara first began driving nights, she had thought of every trip as a list of places she had to reach on time. She still checked the clock, but she now thought just as often about the minutes between stops. On some nights those minutes were enough for a passenger to dry off after the rain or finish a call before going home. On others, they were simply the time it took a bus to get from Ash Lane to the bridge.

At the station, the cleaner got off. The two friends remained, their argument unfinished. One said the ending had been obvious; the other said being obvious did not make it bad. Mara was tempted to ask the name of the film, but the doors opened for four new passengers, and she needed to hear where they were going.

She finished her shift at 1:18, thirteen minutes late. The dispatcher asked whether there had been a problem.

“Nothing much,” Mara said. “A slow boarding at the station.”

She parked in the depot and walked through the bus, checking beneath the seats. She found a receipt, a single glove, and a child’s blue hair clip. All three went into the lost-property box. The bus had picked up that kind of small inventory every night. Someone would be looking for the glove by morning. She hoped the hair clip belonged to someone who had others.

In the drivers’ room, a paper notice on the wall thanked everyone who had worked the 6. Beneath it was a map of Monday’s routes. Mara stood in front of the map while she ate the rest of her roll. The 12 would run down Market Road, as she had told Mrs. Vale. She traced its line with one finger to see where it turned after that. Then she found the 23 and followed the neat loop she would learn next week.

On Monday morning, Mara arrived at the depot early. The yard looked different in daylight: smaller, with oil stains showing clearly beneath the parked buses. Someone was washing a windshield with a long brush. Inside, another driver was filling a travel mug at the sink.

Her new bus smelled faintly of cleaning fluid. Mara adjusted the seat, checked the mirrors, and pulled up the route on the console. At 6:42 she drove out onto the street.

The first passengers were a man going to the supermarket and a woman carrying a stack of folders tied with string. At the school stop, three children boarded together. One had a yellow plaster on his chin. Another counted out his fare in coins while the others waited beside him. Mara gave him time to find the last one at the bottom of his pocket.

As she closed the doors, she noticed the florist from the old shopping district crossing ahead of the bus. Mara recognized her from the late-night window, though she looked different in her coat, with no flowers around her. She was walking quickly toward the bakery.

The light turned green. Mara checked both mirrors and drove on.
